hints: For the box to remain at rest on the $10^\circ$ slope without any applied force, static friction must balance the downhill component of weight: $F = mg\sin 10^\circ$.
The maximum available static friction is $\mu R$, where normal reaction $R = mg\cos 10^\circ$.
Apply the inequality $F \le \mu R$ to show that $\mu \ge \tan 10^\circ \approx 0.176$.
walkthrough: For the box of mass $50\text{ kg}$ to remain stationary on the rough slope of angle $\theta = 10^\circ$, friction must balance the downhill component of gravity.

Resolve perpendicular to the incline:
$$R = mg\cos 10^\circ = 50 \times 10 \times \cos 10^\circ = 500\cos 10^\circ$$

Resolve parallel to the incline:
$$F = mg\sin 10^\circ = 50 \times 10 \times \sin 10^\circ = 500\sin 10^\circ$$

The condition for the box to remain in equilibrium is that the required friction force does not exceed maximum limiting friction:
$$F \le \mu R$$
$$500\sin 10^\circ \le \mu(500\cos 10^\circ)$$

hints: Calculate the work done by the $80\text{ N}$ pushing force over $d = 2.5\text{ m}$: $W_{\text{push}} = 80 \times 2.5 = 200\text{ J}$.
Calculate potential energy lost descending the slope: $mgd\sin 10^\circ = 50(10)(2.5)\sin 10^\circ = 1250\sin 10^\circ$.
Calculate the work done against friction: $W_{\text{fric}} = \mu (500\cos 10^\circ) \times 2.5$ with $\mu = 0.19$.
Apply the work-energy theorem: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = W_{\text{push}} + \text{PE loss} - W_{\text{fric}}$, and solve for speed $v$.
walkthrough:
Use the work-energy principle: initial kinetic energy is zero, so the final kinetic energy equals total positive work done minus work done against friction:
$$E_k = W_{\text{push}} + \text{PE loss} - W_{\text{friction}}$$

1. Calculate work done by the $80\text{ N}$ pushing force along the $2.5\text{ m}$ displacement:
$$W_{\text{push}} = 80 \times 2.5 = 200\text{ J}$$

2. Calculate potential energy lost descending the vertical height $h = 2.5\sin 10^\circ$:
$$\text{PE loss} = mgh = 50 \times 10 \times (2.5\sin 10^\circ) = 1250\sin 10^\circ$$
$$\text{PE loss} = 1250 \times 0.173648 = 217.060\text{ J}$$

3. Calculate the friction force and work done against friction with $\mu = 0.19$:
$$R = mg\cos 10^\circ = 500\cos 10^\circ = 500(0.984808) = 492.404\text{ N}$$
$$F = \mu R = 0.19 \times 492.404 = 93.5568\text{ N}$$
$$W_{\text{friction}} = F \times d = 93.5568 \times 2.5 = 233.892\text{ J}$$

Combine all energy terms to find final kinetic energy:
$$E_k = 200 + 217.060 - 233.892 = 183.168\text{ J}$$

hints: With the plane at $20^\circ$ and no pushing force, the forces along the slope are the downhill component of gravity $mg\sin 20^\circ$ and opposing friction $F = \mu mg\cos 20^\circ$.
Apply Newton's second law down the slope: $mg\sin 20^\circ - \mu mg\cos 20^\circ = ma$.
Cancel mass $m$ to get $a = g\sin 20^\circ - \mu g\cos 20^\circ$, and evaluate using $\mu = 0.19$.
walkthrough: On the steeper slope of angle $\theta = 20^\circ$, no external pushing force acts. The forces acting along the slope are the downward component of gravity and the upward force of friction.

The friction force opposing the downward sliding is:
$$F = \mu R = \mu mg\cos 20^\circ$$

Apply Newton's second law ($F_{\text{net}} = ma$) down the incline:
$$mg\sin 20^\circ - \mu mg\cos 20^\circ = ma$$

Divide every term by mass $m$:
$$a = g\sin 20^\circ - \mu g\cos 20^\circ$$
